sections.text: Nouns of Time and Place
Consider the following sentences:

items.text: — The time of the exam is in the morning.
— The guests sat in the sitting-room.

sections.text: If you reflect on the underlined words, you find them to be nouns derived from verbs: 'mawʿid' is derived from the verb 'waʿada' (to promise) and indicates the time of the appointment; 'al-majlis' is derived from 'jalasa' (to sit) and indicates the place of sitting; and 'al-malʿab' is derived from 'laʿiba' (to play) and indicates the place of playing. For this reason, what indicates time is called ism al-zaman (noun of time), and what indicates place is called ism al-makan (noun of place).
Definition of the Nouns of Time and Place
Ism al-zaman (noun of time): a noun derived from a verb to indicate the time of its occurrence. Ism al-makan (noun of place): a noun derived from a verb to indicate the place of its occurrence.
The noun of time and the noun of place share the very same pattern; only context and the surrounding clues distinguish one from the other.
First: Forming Them from the Triliteral Verb
The nouns of time and place are formed from the triliteral verb on two patterns: 'mafʿal' (with fatha on the ʿayn) and 'mafʿil' (with kasra).
1 – The Pattern mafʿal (with fatha)
The nouns of time and place take the pattern 'mafʿal' when the triliteral verb has fatha or damma on the ʿayn of its present-tense form, or when it is defective (ending in a weak letter).
a – From verbs with fatha on the ʿayn in the present tense:
b – From verbs with damma on the ʿayn in the present tense:
c – From verbs ending in a weak letter (defective verbs); these always take 'mafʿal', whatever the vowel of their present-tense ʿayn:
2 – The Pattern mafʿil (with kasra)

The nouns of time and place take the pattern 'mafʿil' when the triliteral verb has kasra on the ʿayn of its present-tense form, or when it is an assimilated verb beginning with waw (mithal wawi) with a sound final radical.
a – From verbs with kasra on the ʿayn in the present tense:
b – From assimilated verbs beginning with waw whose final radical is sound:

For the hollow verb (with a weak middle radical), the noun follows the present-tense form, and the ʿayn turns into alif or yaʾ: qama, yaqumu / maqam — safa, yasifu / masif (summer resort) — bata, yabitu / mabit (overnight lodging).
Second: Forming Them from Non-Triliteral Verbs

From non-triliteral verbs, the nouns of time and place are formed on the pattern of the passive participle (ism al-mafʿul): take the present-tense form, replace the present-tense prefix with a mim carrying damma, and put fatha on the letter before the last.

Notice that this pattern is the very same as that of the passive participle of non-triliteral verbs; here only context and the sense of the sentence distinguish the passive participle from the nouns of time and place.

items.text: — The awaited time of the guests is after sunset. (noun of time)
— The waiting-place of the travellers is in front of the station. (noun of place)
— Relief is awaited, by Allah's leave. (passive participle)

sections.text: The taʾ Attached to Some Nouns of Place
The taʾ is attached to some nouns of place as heard from the Arabs (samaʿi); no analogy is drawn from them.
How Do We Distinguish the Noun of Time from the Noun of Place?
If the noun of time and the noun of place share one pattern, how do we tell them apart?

We distinguish them by context and the sense of the sentence: if the form indicates the time at which the action occurs, it is a noun of time; if it indicates the spot where it occurs, it is a noun of place. When you say 'mawʿidu-na matlaʿa al-fajri' (our appointment is at daybreak), 'matlaʿ' is a noun of time because it indicates the time of rising; and when you say 'waqaftu fi mawqifi al-sayyarat' (I stood in the car park), 'mawqif' is a noun of place because it indicates the spot of standing.

items.text: — The rising-time of the sun is at dawn. (time)
— Our house is near the mosque. (place)

sections.text: The Difference between Them and the Mimic Masdar
The mimic masdar (al-masdar al-mimi) also comes on the pattern 'mafʿal' or 'mafʿil', but it denotes the action itself, not its time or place; the context is the decisive criterion between them.

items.text: — The masʿa (walking course) is between al-Safa and al-Marwa. (noun of place)
— The benefactor strove a praiseworthy striving. (mimic masdar meaning the act of striving)

sections.text: Summary Table

Do not confuse the nouns of time and place with the passive participle of non-triliteral verbs or with the mimic masdar: the pattern may coincide while the meaning differs, and context alone determines what is intended.
Model Analysis (Iʿrab)

items.text: — The time of the trip is Friday morning.

sections.text: mawʿidu: subject (mubtadaʾ) in the nominative, marked by the visible damma; it is in a construct state, and it is a noun of time on the pattern 'mafʿil'. al-rihlati: second term of the construct (mudaf ilayh) in the genitive, marked by the visible kasra. sabahu: predicate (khabar) in the nominative, marked by the visible damma; it is in a construct state. al-jumuʿati: second term of the construct in the genitive, marked by the visible kasra.
From the Noble Qurʾan
Allah the Exalted said: "He said: Your appointed time is the day of the festival, and that the people be gathered at mid-morning." (Ta-Ha 20:59)

'mawʿidukum': a noun of time on the pattern 'mafʿil' from the assimilated waw-initial verb 'waʿada'; it is a subject (mubtadaʾ) in the nominative marked by the damma, in a construct state, with the attached pronoun in the genitive as the second term; 'yawmu' is the predicate in the nominative marked by the damma, in a construct state, and 'al-zinati' is its second term in the genitive.
And Allah the Exalted said: "Indeed, the righteous will be in a secure place." (Al-Dukhan 44:51)

'maqamin': a noun of place from the hollow verb 'qama'; its origin is 'maqwam' on the pattern 'mafʿal', then the waw turned into alif. The meaning: in a secure place of residing. Its analysis: a noun in the genitive after 'fi', marked by the visible kasra, and 'aminin' is an adjective in the genitive.
